Consult Summary:
- 26-year-old male with asthma presents with 3 hours of chest tightness, mild shortness of breath, wheeze, and cough after recent cold; ran out of inhalers. Plan includes prescription renewal, oral steroids, spacer, and advice on when to seek further care.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Chest tightness for approximately 3 hours.
- Symptoms timeline: Symptoms started today and have persisted for 3 hours; preceded by a cold last week (sore throat, runny nose, general malaise). Runny nose has improved, but cough and chest tightness persist.
- Associated symptoms: Mild shortness of breath (not at rest, worse on exertion, e.g., when walking up stairs), wheeze, cough (non-productive), "tight" feeling, occasional difficulty achieving full breath.
- Systems review: No chest pain, no sputum production. Sore throat and runny nose have improved. Denies shortness of breath at rest.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors: No explicit triggers or relieving measures noted. Symptoms possibly exacerbated by recent lapse in asthma medication use; exertion increases shortness of breath.
- Past severe asthma exacerbation requiring intubation and hospitalization as a teenager (age 16–17); none recently.
- No other acute concerns expressed.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma: Diagnosed in childhood, severe exacerbation requiring intubation and hospitalization in high school. Generally well-controlled on regular inhalers, with rare exacerbations in recent years. Last week without medications due to running out.
- Hay fever (allergic rhinitis).
- Allergy to dust.
- Eczema in childhood.
- Milk protein allergy in childhood (not indicated as current).

Medications:
- Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler – dose/route/frequency not documented; out of supply for approximately one week.
- Clenil Modulite (steroid inhaler) – dose/route/frequency not documented; out of supply for approximately one week.
- No medications currently taken due to running out.
- No known drug allergies.

Social History:
- Student at university (recently away at uni); no further social or occupational details provided.
- No tobacco, alcohol, or substance use history discussed.
- No financial or other lifestyle factors mentioned.

Family History:
- Mother: Eczema.
- Father: Asthma.
- Patient’s own childhood: Eczema, milk protein allergy.

Physical Examination:
- No vitals documented.
- No physical exam findings described.

Investigations:
- No investigations or testing performed or results provided.

Assessment & Plan:

- Issue 1: Asthma exacerbation after recent viral illness and lack of medication
  - Assessment: Asthma exacerbation precipitated by recent viral infection and one-week lapse in inhaler use.
  - Plan:
    - Prescribe Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler.
    - Prescribe Clenil Modulite (steroid inhaler).
    - Prescribe oral steroids (dose: 2 tablets in the morning for 5 days; specific drug and dose not documented).
    - Prescribe spacer device with instructions for use.
    - Advise use of inhalers as directed (Clenil Modulite in the morning; Ventolin as needed when wheezy).
    - Advise seeking immediate medical attention if Ventolin is needed more frequently than every 3 hours, or if symptoms worsen (increased shortness of breath, chest pain, chest tightness, light-headedness).
    - Advise rest and consider time off work until feeling better (can self-certify for up to 7 days).

- General Plan:
    - Advised on steroid side effects (possible mood changes, high blood sugar, rash, nausea, headache; generally well tolerated).
    - Safety net provided: Seek medical care with any deterioration.

●	Missing but clinically expected elements:
   - No medication doses, frequencies, or routes provided.
   - No physical examination or vital signs.
   - No objective assessment (e.g., peak flow, SpO2); unable to perform due to remote consult and lack of device.
   - No documentation of smoking, alcohol, or recreational drug use.
   - No recent hospital or ICU admissions apart from remote history.
   - No work or functional impact assessed in detail.
●	No internal conflicts identified.
●	Transcript quality: Clear and comprehensive; minimal audio interference except for brief connection issue near the end. All information required for safe management addressed within the clinical context.
